fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because honestly I've spent a good chunk of my career building benchmarks, and I've also watched a lot of them get, let's say, over-optimized.

So the first question I ask is, what is the benchmark actually a proxy for? Every benchmark is a stand-in for something we care about in the world. SWE-bench is a stand-in for "can this model do the job of a software engineer." If the improvement you're chasing moves the proxy but not the underlying thing, it's not worth it. And you can usually tell. If the gain comes from a trick that's specific to the format of the benchmark, like exploiting how the evaluation harness scores things, or memorizing patterns in the test set, that's a red flag. If the gain comes from something general, like better reasoning, better tool use, better ability to recover from mistakes, then it probably transfers, and that's worth pursuing.

The second thing is headroom. If a benchmark is at 95 percent, the last few points are almost always noise or label errors. I've looked at enough datasets to know that a few percent of any human-annotated benchmark is just wrong. So fighting over that last stretch is usually a waste. Where things get interesting is the middle of the curve, where models are at 30 or 40 percent and you can actually see qualitative differences in what they can and can't do.

The third thing, and this is maybe the one people underweight, is whether the improvement tells you something. When we built things like WebShop or tau-bench, the goal wasn't really the number. The goal was to have a controlled setting where failures are legible. You can look at a trajectory and say, oh, the model gave up too early, or it hallucinated an API, or it ignored a constraint the user stated. If an improvement on a benchmark comes with that kind of understanding, then even a small gain is valuable because it's pointing at a real capability gap.

And then honestly there's a sociological component. Benchmarks are coordination devices. They let the whole field push in the same direction. So part of judging whether a gain is worth pursuing is asking whether the benchmark is still measuring what the community thinks it measures. Once there's a gap between the number and reality, that's when you need a new benchmark rather than more points on the old one.

So I'd say, pursue improvements when they're general, when there's real headroom, and when the benchmark still has signal. Otherwise your time is better spent building the next one.

r002.rationale: It says there is little value in pursuing the last few points near 95%, and that when the benchmark no longer reflects reality, a new benchmark is needed rather than more points on the old one.

opus-5.5.text:
I usually start by asking whether the benchmark still measures something I actually care about. Benchmarks are proxies. When you design one, you're making a bet that doing well on it correlates with some real capability. Over time that correlation tends to weaken. People find shortcuts, the data leaks into pretraining corpora, or the tasks stop reflecting how the system will really be used. So the first question is whether a point of improvement here still means what it meant when the benchmark came out.

Second, I look at where we are on the curve. If a benchmark sits at 2 or 5 percent, there's a lot of signal: an improvement often means you've unlocked something qualitatively new. If it's at 90-plus, you're often fitting noise, label errors, or quirks of the test set, and the marginal gain tells you little about the underlying capability. That's partly why, with SWE-bench, we grounded the tasks in real GitHub issues and real repositories. We wanted something hard enough to stay informative for a while, and close enough to actual software engineering that progress on it would plausibly transfer.

Third, I ask how the improvement was achieved. Did you get there through a general idea, like better reasoning, better use of feedback from the environment, or better tool use? Or did you engineer around the specific structure of the benchmark? The first kind of gain tends to carry over to other tasks. The second usually doesn't, and it can actively mislead the field. A good sanity check is whether the same method helps on a related benchmark it wasn't tuned for.

The last thing, which I think gets underrated, is reliability. For agents especially, average success rate isn't the whole story. If a system solves a task once out of ten tries, that's very different from solving it ten out of ten. That was a big motivation behind how we measured things in tau-bench, looking at consistency across repeated trials rather than just pass@1. An improvement that makes a system dependable is often worth more than one that bumps the headline number but leaves it brittle.

So my rough heuristic is: is the benchmark still faithful to the capability, is there real headroom, is the method general, and does it make the system more reliable? If the answer to most of those is yes, it's worth pursuing. If not, you may just be climbing a leaderboard.

r002.rationale: It questions whether a benchmark remains informative, but does not recommend shifting attention to a new challenge when it becomes saturated.

fable-5.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, because benchmarks are really the currency of progress in our field, and it's easy to get caught up chasing numbers without asking what they mean.

For me, there are a few tests. The first is whether the benchmark still measures what it was designed to measure. Early on, a benchmark usually captures a genuine capability gap — when we built things like SWE-bench, the gap between what models could do and what the benchmark asked was enormous, so any real improvement there told you something about actual software engineering ability. But as the community optimizes against a benchmark, you start getting improvements that are specific to the benchmark rather than the underlying skill. People overfit to the distribution of problems, to quirks in the evaluation harness, even to contamination in training data. At that point, going from 85 to 87 percent might mean nothing, whereas earlier, going from 20 to 30 percent meant a lot.

The second test is whether the improvement transfers. If a technique moves one benchmark but nothing else, I'm skeptical. The improvements worth pursuing tend to lift a whole family of tasks, because they reflect something general — better reasoning, better grounding, better ability to recover from mistakes. That's part of why I've gravitated toward agentic benchmarks, where the model has to interact with an environment over many steps. It's much harder to game multi-step interaction than a static multiple-choice question, so gains there tend to be more meaningful.

And the third, honestly, is just asking: if we saturate this benchmark, does the world change? Does anyone's workflow get better? If the answer is yes, the headroom is worth fighting for even if progress is slow. If the answer is no — if it's a leaderboard that matters only to the people on it — then the effort is probably better spent building a new benchmark that recreates that gap between what we can measure and what we actually want. In some sense, the most valuable moment in a benchmark's life is right after it's created, when it's exposing a real weakness. Our job is to keep creating those moments, not just to climb.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a 20-to-30% gain as meaningful with an 85-to-87% gain as potentially meaningless, clearly presenting larger gains as stronger progress signals near saturation.

r002.rationale: It recommends building a new benchmark when saturating the current one would not change the world. It says continued progress is worth pursuing when saturation would improve workflows, so it does not recommend shifting to a new challenge whenever a benchmark becomes saturated.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, the first question I ask is whether the benchmark is measuring something I'd care about if the benchmark didn't exist. A lot of the time we've built these datasets as proxies for a capability — reasoning, grounding, long-horizon planning — and then the proxy becomes the goal, and people optimize the proxy in ways that don't move the thing underneath at all. So I try to be very explicit: what's the real-world task I think this stands in for, and if I got five points, would anybody downstream notice?

The second thing is the nature of the gain. If the method that produces the improvement is narrow — some clever prompt scaffolding or a loss term tuned to that distribution — I'm much less interested, even if the number is big. Whereas a smaller gain from something that's general, that you'd expect to also help on three tasks you didn't test, that's worth a lot more. The transfer is the signal, not the delta.

And then there's headroom. On a lot of benchmarks we're in the regime where the remaining errors are label noise or ambiguity in the annotation, and you're just fitting the idiosyncrasies of whoever wrote the dataset. I've spent a fair amount of time hand-reading the examples a model still gets wrong, and that's usually how you find out — are these genuinely hard instances, or is the benchmark just done? If it's done, the right move is to go build a harder measurement, not to grind out another point.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I start by asking whether the benchmark is a good proxy for something I actually care about. If it's a task where a gain would change what people can do with these systems, like fixing real software issues or handling a customer's request end to end, then progress is worth chasing. If it's a narrow format where the score can go up without the system getting more useful, I'm much more skeptical.

I look at three things.

First, does the improvement come from something general? If a method helps across several benchmarks, models, and settings, that tells me it's capturing a real capability. If it only moves one number, and especially if it depends on tricks specific to that benchmark's format, I suspect we're overfitting to the test.

Second, is there still headroom, and is the remaining error interesting? Once a benchmark is near saturation, the last few points are often noise, annotation errors, or contamination. But if models fail in systematic ways, like long-horizon planning, using tools reliably, or recovering from their own mistakes, then working on those failures teaches us something.

Third, I try to look past the aggregate score and read the failures. Two systems can get the same accuracy for very different reasons. Reading the trajectories tells you whether the model is reasoning or exploiting a quirk of the data.

I also think researchers should hold themselves to the standard that a benchmark is a measuring instrument, not the goal. The best ones, once models improve, get replaced by harder ones that reflect what we want. So I'd say an improvement is worth pursuing when it gets us closer to that underlying capability, and not just when it moves the leaderboard.

haiku-5.5.text:
That's a question I keep coming back to. The first thing I check is whether the benchmark measures what we actually care about, or a proxy that's become easy to game. A lot of leaderboard movement comes from models learning the test's format or from test data leaking into training. Before I get excited about a jump, I want to know whether it's a broad gain across different kinds of problems or a spike on one narrow slice.

Second, I look at the size of the gain relative to noise. A point or two on a small eval from a single run isn't much of a finding. If the improvement holds across seeds, on held-out variants, and when the questions are reworded, that's far more interesting.

Third, I ask whether the gain transfers. If a change makes a model better at one benchmark but doesn't show up anywhere else, we may have optimized the measurement rather than the model. The improvements I most want to chase are the ones that carry over to problems the benchmark's authors didn't anticipate.

Finally, there's cost. Some gains are cheap and tell you something real about why the model behaves the way it does. Others take an enormous amount of compute for a marginal number. I'd rather spend effort on the first kind, because when you understand why something improved, that understanding tends to help with the next problem too.

I think the first question is: what does the improvement actually tell us? A benchmark is a proxy for some capability we care about. So if the score goes up, I want to understand whether the model has become better at that capability, and whether that carries over to new situations.

A small improvement can be really interesting if it comes from an idea that addresses a fundamental limitation. And a much larger improvement can be less interesting if it depends on something very specific to that dataset.

So I’d look at the errors, look at what changed, and test the idea under different conditions. For me, the most compelling reason to keep pursuing a benchmark is that it’s still helping us ask useful scientific questions—not simply that there’s room to move the number.

So I’d look at what actually changed. Can the model now handle a class of problems it couldn’t handle before? Does the improvement carry over to different settings? And can we understand why the method helped? A small improvement can be quite interesting if it reveals something useful about learning or generalization.

I also think you have to look at the examples. An aggregate score can hide a lot. If you inspect the failures, you might discover that there’s a fundamental limitation that the benchmark isn’t really capturing. At that point, developing a better way to measure the capability might be more valuable than pushing the existing score a little higher.
